content:
In today's hearing, Apple is challenging the UK government's refusal to publicly confirm whether it has issued a request to access encrypted user data. Here are the relevant details.

A little background

Earlier last year, The Washington Post reported that the UK government had secretly ordered Apple to build a backdoor into all content uploaded by iCloud users worldwide.

The order itself is also subject to strict secrecy provisions, with Apple even prohibited from publicly confirming or discussing the request.

The UK government consistently adopts a policy of neither confirming nor denying, refusing to confirm or deny the existence of any such individual order, while companies that receive such orders are also restricted from disclosing the fact that they have received an order.

Due to this reportedly existing but never officially confirmed order, Apple withdrew the option of enabling "Advanced Data Protection" (ADP) for UK iCloud users.

The reason is that once ADP is enabled, iCloud backups and other iCloud data categories will be protected by end-to-end encryption. Therefore, Apple refused to comply with the UK's backdoor order and simply stopped offering ADP to new UK users, even though the original order reportedly applied to global users.

At this stage, the tug-of-war between Apple and the UK government has two fronts: on one hand, Apple is challenging the fundamental request to access encrypted data; on the other, it is challenging the gag order prohibiting it from publicly discussing the request.

In April 2025, a judge rejected the UK government's attempt to keep the basic details of Apple's legal challenge secret, ruling that disclosing the existence of the case would not harm national security.

A few months later, under pressure from the White House, the UK government dropped its demand for access to US user data in the secret order. However, the demand has not completely disappeared: the UK subsequently issued a new notice targeting Apple users within the UK.

Fast forward to a few weeks ago, it was reported that Apple had launched a second legal challenge against the UK government after the original global order was replaced by a new order targeting UK users.

That brings us to today's news.

Apple challenges the secrecy arrangements of the order

According to Reuters, Apple challenged the UK government's continued refusal to confirm or deny the existence of a new "Technical Capability Notice" at a hearing at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) in London today.

According to Reuters, Apple's lawyers pointed out that the government's confidentiality policy makes meaningful public discussion of the case impossible and undermines the principle of open justice.

Quoted from the report:

At the hearing held on Thursday at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, Ben Jaffey, a lawyer representing the advocacy groups "Privacy International" and "Liberty," said the government's position had become "absurd." He said: "The horse has bolted long ago," meaning the relevant information has long been public. He pointed out that US politicians and officials had publicly mentioned the original notice, and unnamed UK government sources had also confirmed it to the media. Both he and Apple's lawyers believe that the UK government's "neither confirm nor deny" policy is an insult to open justice and hinders meaningful public discussion on the matter.

To be clear, the focus of today's hearing is the secrecy of the order, not whether the UK government actually has the legal power to demand access to Apple's encrypted data.

After today's hearing, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal will decide whether the government can continue to rely on its "neither confirm nor deny" policy in this case. Reuters noted that a formal hearing on Apple's legal challenge to the Technical Capability Notice itself is unlikely to take place before next year.
